finding.claim: The purge handler calls checkPerm(u, "admin") but discards the boolean result, so the admin check is never enforced. Any caller who reaches the handler can run purgeAll(). This is a missing authorization check. rotateKeys uses mustPerm correctly and returns on failure.
finding.source: Any authenticated (or otherwise able to reach the route) non-admin user sends an HTTP request to the purge endpoint.
finding.sink: purgeAll() at handlers.go:27, a destructive admin-only operation.

trace.note: u := userFrom(r) loads the requesting user from context
checkPerm(u, "admin") returns false for a non-admin, but the return value is ignored

finding.guards_checked: checkPerm returns a bool and does not write a response or abort. There is no if/return on its result in purge. Only handlers.go exists, so no router-level middleware was visible. The only permission guard in the file is mustPerm, which purge does not use. By contrast, rotateKeys at line 33 uses mustPerm and returns on failure.

verdict.guard_found: none. checkPerm (handlers.go:12-14) returns a bool and does not write a response or abort. Its result is discarded at line 26. mustPerm is only used in rotateKeys (line 33). No router or middleware is visible; handlers.go is the only source file.
verdict.reason: handlers.go:26 calls checkPerm(u, "admin") as a bare statement and ignores the bool it returns, so purgeAll() at handlers.go:27 runs for any caller who reaches the route, including a non-admin. rotateKeys at handlers.go:33-35 tests mustPerm and returns on failure, so the two handlers differ.

verdict_facts.guard_found: checkPerm (handlers.go:12) returns a bool, and purge discards it at line 26. No router-level or other middleware is visible in the directory. mustPerm is the enforcing variant, but only rotateKeys uses it.
